newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Strikebound BA seeks union talks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Strikebound BA seeks union talks.

text.p: British Airways on Thursday called on striking cabin crew to reopen talks over pay and a cost-saving plan to save 42 million pounds ($70.8 million) as the two-day-old disruption continued to ground flights and strand thousands of passengers, despite the airline threatening legal action.
But BA said it expected to see continued improvement in services operating on Friday after it increased its services by 25 percent on Thursday from Wednesday.

However the airline expected disruption to spill over into the weekend before services got back to normal, with only 75 percent of all its longhaul flights likely to operate and 50 percent of shorthaul on Saturday.
There was no contact between the management and unions today, effectively ending hopes that the strike could be called off before Friday.

Mike Street, BA director of operations, told a news conference he was urging the British Airways Stewards and Stewardesses Association (BASSA) to hold fresh talks with management over pay deal which a breakaway cabin crew union, Cabin Crew 89, has already accepted.

"We have an opportunity now to sort out the strike with BASSA. We have to have a better relationship...we're ready at any time to sit down and talk, but we won't unpick a deal we've discussed (with unions) over five months," Street said.

Management has warned that employees face loss of travel perks and opportunities of promotion if they went on strike. It has also threatened to sack or even sue individual strikers -- tactics which the unions have termed "intimidatory" and "macho".

As BA turned up the heat on strikers with threats of legal action and of bringing in newly-recruited staff replacements, it said it had chartered seven aircraft and was offering cabin crew taxis and hotel accommodation to ensure they turned up for work on Friday.

George Ryde, the Transport & General Workers Union (T&G) union's senior official said chartering aircraft would make little difference to the impact of the strike, which he said received "solid support".
"The turn out has been brilliant," he told the UK Press Association news agency.

BA meanwhile claimed some 1,600 staff had come into work on Thursday while only 250 had gone on strike. But a further 1,700 have so far called to say they would not be coming in for work, rather than admit they were striking for fear of reprisals from the airline.
BA's Street estimated the strike had already cost the carrier "considerably more than the pilots' dispute last year which didn't even become a strike".
The pilots' dispute is estimated to have cost BA 15 million pounds.

BA claims the strike over allowances and overtime and its plans to cut costs from its operating budget is illegal because of a discrepancy in the strike ballot, which it says, canvassed more cabin crew than were actually on the company pay roll.
"We are in touch with our lawyers and we've told the union we reserve our legal right to take action," Mervyn Walker, BA director of human resources, said.
The T&G's Ryde however said earlier he was confident the strike ballot was legal and the union would win any legal action if a challenge was mounted by BA.

Paul Nicholls, an expert on industrial relations at Dibb Lupton Alsop, a UK legal firm, said the British High Court was likely to take a strict view of any discrepancy in strike balloting and could award BA up to 250,000 pounds damages plus costs if the action was successful.

"This (the threat of action) is obviously another weapon that BA is bringing to the negotiating table...But if you have to ask why (BA) hasn't already taken legal action or served an injunction to stop the strike if it's right (about balloting)," Nicholls said in an interview.
BA has run into conflict with its employees over a programme to cut one billion pounds in costs by 2000.

The T&G says it will call another 72-hour strike if no agreement is reached with management. BA says the "ball is firmly in the unions' court" regarding the new pay agreement and the plan to save 42 million pounds.
The T&G says it is prepared to help the airline find the money, but it was not prepared to have new terms and conditions imposed on its members.
BA's Street said far fewer passengers had been stranded than the 25,000 on Wednesday because they had been given more notice to make other arrangements and more services had been laid on.

Meanwhile, a decision is expected later today from BA ground staff belonging to the T&G on whether to stage a separate strike in protest at the sale of the airline's catering operation at London Heathrow.

The industrial action is part of a war BA is fighting on several fronts. The carrier is striving to get clearance for a massive alliance with American Airlines, while also fighting off a legal challenge from Laker Airway Inc in Florida.
($ = 0.593 British Pounds)
